newsitem.title: USA: Ramco chief sees some Caspian production 1-2 years.
newsitem.headline: Ramco chief sees some Caspian production 1-2 years.

text.p: Ramco Energy Plc expects to begin oil production in the Shallow Gunashli field in the Caspian Sea off the Azeri coast in the next 12 to 24 months, company chairman Steve Remp said.

Remp, in remarks at an American Stock Exchange conference Wednesday, said his Aberdeen, Scotland-based company would have oil available from the Caspian well before production from the other massive oil fields there comes one line.
A consortium of companies, headed by British Petroleum and Norway's Statoil, is currently negotiating to set up production and pipeline operations in the region.

Remp did not say how large a stake Ramco would have in the Shallow Gunashli field, though he said Conoco Inc was also seeking a share in the field to help rehabilitate the facilities run by SOCAR, the Azeri state oil company.
Conoco refused to confirm their interest in the field, though a spokesman said the company was pursuing interests in the region.
The Shallow Gunashli, at the north end of the larger Caspian oil deposit, has an estimated 520 million barrels in cumulative production available.

Up through 1989 the Shallow Gunashli field produced 112,000 barrels per day, but SOCAR's production reached "the outer boundaries of what the Azeris could produce technically," Remp said. Sources estimated the field's current output at about 100,000 bpd.

Ramco is the tiniest member of Caspian Sea consortium, the Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC), which includes Exxon, Amoco, British Petroleum, Statoil, Itochu, Lukoil, Pennzoil, Unocal, Delta Nimir Khazar Limited, Turkish Petroleum and SOCAR.

The entire Caspian oil field, which incorporates the Gunashli, the Shallow Gunashli, the Chirag and Azeri fields, measures 30 miles long by three to five miles wide, according to Remp, and the consortium will spend about $10 billion, excluding pipeline costs, to exploit the region over the next 30 years.
"A stake at this table is something every company would like to have," Remp said. "It will be a political and economic force in its own right."
